name: Accounting firm practice and tax prep
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: The category is less legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. The incumbents are vendor-updated desktop products on annual licences, not self-run mainframe code, and firms can switch at any season boundary. The lock-in comes from prior-year data rollover, form coverage and busy-season risk, not from scarce skills or long contracts.

name: Agriculture and commodity trading
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The core is 1980s-90s Windows client-server rather than mainframe, and its vendors keep modernising it in place (SQL, hosted versions) while overlays like Bushel and Covantis work around it. That makes the category less locked-in on platform and skills than mainframe-heavy categories. The paper, email and spreadsheet workarounds are more severe than typical.

name: Airline reservations and passenger service
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less legacy-locked at the runtime than a typical enterprise category, because the two dominant PSS vendors (Amadeus by 2018, Sabre mostly by 2024) have already moved their own hosts off the mainframe and run them as multi-tenant hosted services. More locked at the contract and data-model level than most: a vendor switch is a multi-year, airline-wide cutover through IATA PNR, EDIFACT and interline plumbing.

name: AML, KYC and financial-crime compliance (transaction monitoring, screening, case management)
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software because regulators have validated the rule scenarios and payment-message filters, and switching means re-tuning, back-testing and parallel runs under enforcement risk. It is less legacy in technology terms: the engines are 2000s-era Java/SAS, cloud vendors such as Verafin already dominate the small-bank segment, and incumbents are moving their own products to cloud.

name: Capital markets trading, clearing and brokerage back-office
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software. Its cores are regulator-gated network utilities (exchanges, clearing houses, depositories), and every link to them must be re-certified, so failed replacements like ASX CHESS cost hundreds of millions and are public. But the end-user broker layer already has well-funded cloud-native challengers (Apex, Alpaca, DriveWealth, Clear Street), which makes it less locked than core banking.

name: Card issuing and payments processing
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A handful of 1990s-era mainframe and NonStop platforms (TS2, VisionPLUS/Optis, BASE24) process most cards at the largest issuers, under 3-to-10-year processing contracts with penalties and scheme certifications. But cloud processors (Marqeta, Thredd, Pismo, Zeta) have already won the greenfield fintech segment, so the lock-in is concentrated at incumbent banks.

name: Civil registration, vital statistics and national ID systems
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software on replacement timelines, because statutory record validity, centuries of paper and microfilm conversion, and 12-year PPP operator concessions stretch every migration. It is less locked on the technology itself, because most cores are vendor-maintained COTS or national platforms re-platformed in the 2000s-2010s, not untouched mainframes.

name: Construction project accounting
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software because decades of job-cost, certified/union payroll and WIP/surety reporting history sit in pre-2005 client-server cores (Timberline, Viewpoint, COINS). It is less locked than mainframe categories because those cores run on mainstream Windows/SQL, get hosted, and are routinely bolted onto by cloud overlays instead of ripped out.

name: Cooperative, rural and microfinance banking (core + ERP for small lenders)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Fiserv and Jack Henry midrange cores dominate US credit unions and community banks under 7+ year outsourced contracts. In Germany and India, group utilities and government mandates fix the platform. Small Asian lenders lack the capital and staff to migrate.

name: Core banking
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Core banking is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software: it is the regulated system of record. 61% of US banks have kept the same core provider for 10+ years, and failed migrations draw public fines (TSB, GBP48.65M). The lock-in is softer in Asia, where most installed cores are 1997-2003 Java/Oracle products (Finacle, FLEXCUBE, T24) rather than mainframe or RPG.

name: Courts and justice case management
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than typical enterprise software, because each jurisdiction is a single sovereign buyer. It works on annual appropriations, has statutory record and judicial-consensus constraints, and depends on many interfaces to police, prosecutors and DMV. Rollouts take a decade. It is less mainframe-bound than banking or tax, since much of the US moved onto 2003-era vendor platforms (Tyler, Journal Technologies) and most Asian judiciaries built post-2007 systems.

name: E-invoicing and indirect-tax compliance (clearance e-invoice, VAT/GST reporting)
reason: no strong sign
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category: most clearance e-invoicing systems were built after 2010 in response to new mandates (Peppol networks, government portals, SaaS APIs), and only the US tax-engine layer (Vertex L Series, Taxware) and its SAP ECC coupling carry real pre-2005 lock-in.

name: Hospital records (EHR)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital EHRs are more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software on age and replacement time: M/MUMPS and 1990s client-server cores, 10-year contracts, and multi-billion-dollar multi-year cutovers. But the dominant vendor (Epic) is gaining share and keeps its skill pipeline fed, so skill scarcity is weaker than in mainframe categories.

name: Wholesale distribution ERP
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Most installed systems are mid-market products on Windows/SQL Server or Progress, so they can be replaced in 12 to 18 months, and Epicor and Infor are pushing customers to their own cloud versions. Pockets of real lock-in remain: UniVerse/Pick (Eclipse) and RPG (A+), plus decades of contract-pricing logic.

name: Manufacturing ERP
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Manufacturing ERP is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category because the core is wired into plant-floor equipment, MES, OEM EDI and traceability records, so cutover means risking a production stop. That keeps decades-old SAP ECC, IBM i RPG and Progress 4GL systems running long after vendor deadlines, even though SMB manufacturers are moving quickly to cloud MRP.

name: Field service and maintenance (EAM/CMMS)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category. The dominant EAM cores are old, but they run on mainstream Java and ABAP, upgrade in months, and leave much of the market (SMB plants) with no system at all, so cloud CMMS can win greenfield without displacing anything.

name: Financial close and general ledger
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The installed base sits on 1990s cores (SAP ECC, Oracle EBS, JD Edwards) kept in place by audit, SOX and statutory-reporting risk, but close-overlay tools and fast mid-market migrations let firms work around the GL rather than being locked in, so it is less locked than the core banking or mainframe categories.

name: Freight forwarding and customs brokerage
reason: no strong sign
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category on technology, because the dominant platform (CargoWise) is a continuously updated vendor-hosted codebase. Lock-in comes instead from per-country customs-filing certifications, partner network effects and vendor consolidation (WiseTech now owns Kewill/BluJay/e2open), while the truly old tech sits in government filing gateways.

name: Government benefits and social security
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. National benefit cores are bespoke government COBOL/mainframe builds that hard-code statutory payment rules, and they cannot pause payments to migrate. That makes rewrites decade-long and politically risky. There is no off-the-shelf SaaS replacement market.

name: Licensing, permits and case management
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is less locked than core banking or mainframe tax because the leading platforms run on mainstream Java or .NET stacks with vendor SaaS migration paths, few hard skills shortages, and 3-to-5-year contracts. It is more locked than typical SaaS categories because statutory workflows, fee schedules and decades of parcel and case history sit in proprietary schemas held by about 90,000 fragmented local buyers (in ASEAN, by a few national platforms).

name: Government tax administration
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Tax administration is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software at the national level in the US, UK and AU. Each agency is a single sovereign buyer that cannot interrupt revenue collection, and it carries decades of annually amended tax law encoded in COBOL. It is less locked in SEA, where Vietnam, Indonesia and India replaced their cores between 2014 and 2025.

name: Hotel property management
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: Hotel PMS is LESS legacy-locked than typical enterprise software: the old core is 1990s client-server on Oracle DB rather than mainframe, individual properties cut over in weeks, cloud challengers (Mews, Cloudbeds, Apaleo, HotelKey) already hold tens of thousands of properties, and the remaining lock-in comes mostly from chain brand mandates and interface webs rather than scarce skills or decade-long contracts.

name: Insurance claims management
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Claims is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Systems hold open reserves, litigation files and regulator-mandated history that must be migrated intact, and they connect to policy, payments, reinsurance and fraud tools. Unlike policy admin, though, claims is often the first core module carriers replace, and AI overlays (fraud, triage, damage estimation) can sit on top of the incumbent without replacing it.

name: Insurance policy administration
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category because life and annuity policies stay in force for decades. Insurers have to keep servicing closed books on the original mainframe or AS/400 PAS, and many run several PAS at once. P&C is the exception: Tier-1 carriers there have largely moved to post-2005 cores such as Guidewire and Duck Creek.

name: Laboratory information systems
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: LIS is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Every change has to be revalidated under CLIA, CAP or ISO 15189, blood-bank modules are FDA-regulated devices, and decades of analyzer interfaces build up. In US hospitals, though, the systems are being replaced faster than in most legacy categories, because LIS moves with the EHR into Epic Beaker.

name: Land and property registry
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The register carries a state guarantee of title and is bound to local land law. That makes it more locked in than typical enterprise software: replacements need statutory change, decades-long concessions and bulk data migration. But the cores are mostly bespoke systems from around 2000 rather than COBOL, so the skills risk is lower than in banking or tax.

name: Law firm practice management
reason: no strong sign
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category: the cores are Windows/.NET/SQL Server products whose own vendors offer lift-and-shift cloud hosting (3E cloud, Expert Sierra), and the SMB tier is being replaced quickly by cloud-native tools (Clio, Filevine, Smokeball). The lock-in that remains comes from trust-accounting rules and decades of customised billing integrations, not from obsolete technology or scarce skills.

name: Loan origination and servicing
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical in US mortgage servicing, where one 1960s-era mainframe (MSP) holds 63% of first-lien loans with 5 to 7 year contracts. It is less locked in origination, where Encompass and newer LOS and lending platforms are already cloud-hosted and challengers (nCino, Lentra, Mambu) are winning share.

name: Custom COBOL and mainframe applications (cross-industry)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category: the dominant stack (z/OS, CICS, IMS, COBOL) dates from the 1960s and holds decades of undocumented business rules, and the vendor still ships new hardware every year, so staying put is cheaper and less risky than migrating.

name: Medical billing and revenue cycle
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital RCM is more locked in than typical enterprise software because billing shares one M-based database with the EHR, so replacing billing means replacing the EHR. But the dominant cores are still actively developed, and most of the manual pain comes from payer connectivity, not the cores' age.

name: Mortgage servicing
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Mortgage servicing is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category because one vendor-hosted COBOL/CICS mainframe system (ICE MSP) runs roughly half or more of US mortgage loans, and network effects across subservicers, MSR transfers and GSE reporting make leaving costly. That lock-in is mostly a US phenomenon: elsewhere servicing sits inside general core-banking or lending suites.

name: Payroll and HR administration
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Payroll is more locked-in than typical enterprise software at the deep end: statutory tax, award and union rules are hard-coded, errors are not tolerated, and the evidence shows multi-year, billion-dollar public-sector replacements. It is less locked-in at the top and the bottom, where Workday (65%+ of the Fortune 500) and SaaS bureaus such as ADP RUN and Gusto already hold much of the installed base.

name: Pension, provident fund and superannuation administration
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Decades of member benefit history and statutory rules must be migrated exactly, and many dominant buyers are single government funds, so replacement takes 5 to 15 years. Australia's super market is the exception: post-2010 platforms and frequent fund mergers make it less locked-in.

name: Pharmacy management
reason: no strong sign
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. The buyers are mostly independent pharmacies that switch vendor-hosted PMS products through routine conversions. The lock-in comes from payer/PBM and NHS EPS certification, records migration and vendor consolidation (RedSail ~16,000 US pharmacies), not from old code or scarce skills. Government hospital systems such as VA VistA and Malaysia PhIS are the exception.

name: Port and container terminal operating systems (TOS)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A TOS is real-time control of cranes, gates and automated equipment, so cutovers need operational shutdowns and cores run 20 to 30 years. It is less locked than mainframe categories, because the dominant product (Navis N4, 2006) is a vendor-supported Java platform that gets regular upgrades and is moving to cloud.

name: Procurement and accounts payable
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software at the core, because purchasing and AP sit inside the ERP system of record (SAP ECC, Oracle EBS) and replacing them takes years. It is less locked in at the edges, because cloud P2P and AP-automation overlays bolt on easily and the clerk-level skills stay plentiful.

name: Real estate property management
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category in the US mid-market, where cloud-native AppFolio and Entrata hold large shares and the incumbents host their old cores as SaaS. Pockets are more locked: trust-accounting desktop software in Australia, UK social-housing HMS (OHMS on Solaris), and SAP RE-FX tied to S/4HANA deadlines.

name: Regulatory and prudential reporting (bank/insurer/fund returns to regulators)
reason: evidence too thin: strong + half weak below 2.5
differentiator: Less locked in than a typical enterprise category on the software itself. The regulator controls the format and forces periodic re-platforming (D2A to APRA Connect, OSCA to BEEDS, RBI XBRL to CIMS), and the engines are modern stacks without scarce skills. More locked in on process: the reporting logic is spread across upstream data lineage and spreadsheet last-mile work that banks avoid touching because errors draw penalties.

name: Retail point of sale and merchandising
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is less locked in than a typical enterprise one at the till: store POS gets replaced in months on a 5 to 7 year hardware cycle, and SMBs are moving straight to cloud POS. It is more locked in at the merchandising core (RMS, MMS on IBM i, SAP IS-Retail, homegrown systems), where custom pricing and inventory logic makes replacement risky, as Lidl's failed EUR 500M project shows.

name: Student information systems
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software in higher ed: 1980s-90s cores still run at about a third of North American institutions, and the fixed academic calendar plus regulator reporting (IPEDS, HESA, PDDikti) stretch replacement to 5+ years. It is less locked in K-12, where cloud MIS vendors took most of the English schools market within a decade.

name: Telecom billing and BSS
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Billing is more locked in than most enterprise software: a handful of incumbents (Amdocs, CSG, Ericsson, Oracle) bill on 15- to 35-year relationships, and every failed cutover hits revenue directly. The lock-in comes from contracts and embedded tariff logic more than from scarce COBOL skills, because most cores are Oracle/C++/Java rather than mainframe.

name: Trade finance
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category on the core platform. A few 1980s-1990s engines (IMEX, Trade Innovation, Eximbills) dominate, and live multi-year instruments make migration hard. But much of the manual work comes from paper trade documents and UCP rules rather than from the software, so the workaround and skills signs are weaker than the platform sign.

name: Transport management
reason: no strong sign
differentiator: Less legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category: shipper-side TMS has largely moved to SaaS (about 60%+ of the market), and most small fleets worldwide never had a TMS. The real legacy pocket is North American carrier dispatch on IBM i and on-prem client-server (TL2000, Innovative IES, McLeod, TMW.Suite) plus SAP ECC/TM 9.x shops facing the 2027 deadline.

name: Utility billing and customer information
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Billing is regulated and revenue-critical, and failed cutovers are publicly costly (LADWP went from $87M to about $181M). SAP's 2027/2030 IS-U deadline forces decade-long replacement contracts, though Kraken's 70M+ cloud accounts show competitive retail energy is migrating faster than municipal water and power.

name: Warehouse management
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category's legacy pool is pinned to on-prem ERP and IBM i cores, with a hard SAP LE-WM support deadline in 2027. But green-screen RF flows are cheap to reskin, and SaaS WMS is already taking much of the mid-market, so lock-in is weaker than in core banking or mainframe insurance.

name: Wealth and portfolio accounting
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software at the bank, trust and fund-accounting core: a mainframe COBOL engine (InvestOne) still keeps the books for most mutual funds, and audited performance history is hard to migrate. It is less locked at the RIA and family-office end, where cloud aggregators (Addepar, Orion, Black Diamond) already dominate new installs.
